faults.quote: I don't have total passengers flown and average fare per passenger.
faults.why: The case holds fares by route (Lakeport, Port Avery) and seats and load factor, so passengers per flight can be derived. These reached the candidate on Exhibit 2 two turns later, so the flat refusal was false.

faults.quote: As the exhibit shows: A Hub–Lakeport flight has 80 seats and there are 2,000 of them a year, and the load factor was 75% in both FY2023 and FY2025.
faults.why: The candidate asked whether the 75% load factor would hold at a $140 fare. The interviewer repeated the historical load-factor line already on Exhibit 2, which does not answer the hypothetical, and gave no 'I don't have that'.

faults.quote: All nine aircraft are leased through 2030, so returning them early is not an option.
faults.why: The candidate asked for a breakdown of the $20M showing how much is aircraft leases. The lease-term line answers whether leases can be deferred, but the dollar split goes unanswered with no 'I don't have the breakdown'.

faults.quote: How do you read those numbers?
faults.why: The released line is qualitative (lease term), not a set of numbers, so the question reads wrong.

faults.quote: What else could Larkspur do to make sure it's profitable in the first year?
faults.why: At t21 the candidate claimed roughly $5 more per passenger is needed to clear the $0.2M gap; the right figure is about $0.83. That claim was never probed or corrected; only the load-factor claim was probed later.

faults.quote: What would you do to guard against that?
faults.why: In t29 the candidate had just answered what they would do about the competitor following (defensible pricing, loyalty, slots, a trigger). The follow-up re-asks the mitigation, which t28 had also already asked.
